passage: In the robotics club room, Raghav clicked to his last slide and waited. "This is lazy," Hemant said, not looking up from his phone. "Your budget doesn't add up and you've hidden it behind a nice chart." Two juniors stared at the floor. Raghav's ears burned. He mumbled "okay, sir" and walked out to the stairwell, thinking of quitting the club and telling everyone that Hemant just enjoyed being harsh. Then he counted the budget on his fingers. One whole line was off. That part was true, even if the tone still rankled. He went back in, sat down and said, "Sir, I found the error. What else looks weak?" Hemant grunted. "Second slide. Start there."

qa.q: Where did Raghav go after hearing the feedback?
qa.a: He walked out to the stairwell.

qa.q: What was Raghav tempted to do in the stairwell, and what does that say about his feelings?
qa.a: He thought of quitting the club and blaming Hemant for enjoying being harsh, which shows hurt and irritation.

qa.q: How did Raghav separate the delivery from the content?
qa.a: He checked the budget himself, found the real error, and went back to ask what else was weak.

qa.q: How might the two juniors have felt during the feedback?
qa.a: They stared at the floor, which suggests they felt uneasy and maybe worried about their own turn.

grounding: A mentor is blunt and it stings; the student uses what is true and does not quit or hold a grudge.

passage: Parul caught Vasudha outside the hostel mess in Pune with a printout of her internship options. "Didi, you know everything. Which one should I take?" Vasudha felt a pleasant flutter at hearing it. She could have simply announced an answer. Instead she read the three offers and said, "I know how the first company runs, because I did it last summer. The other two I've never seen, so don't take my word about them." Then she asked, "What do you want to learn?" Parul chewed her pen. "Maybe design work, not just testing." "Then write to the second one and ask what interns actually do. Tell me what they say." Walking to her room, Vasudha thought that Parul would make her own call, and that felt better than being the expert.

qa.q: Where did Parul catch Vasudha?
qa.a: She caught Vasudha outside the hostel mess in Pune.

qa.q: What did Vasudha feel when Parul said she knew everything, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt a pleasant flutter but did not use it to announce an answer; she said which offers she knew and asked what Parul wanted to learn.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Vasudha to say she had never seen two of the companies?
qa.a: It kept Parul from trusting guesses as facts and pointed her to ask the company herself. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Parul when Vasudha asks what she wants to learn?
qa.a: Parul has to think about her own wishes, and her answer about design work shows she has a view of her own.

grounding: A junior asks for guidance; the senior shares what she knows, admits what she does not and encourages the junior's own view.

passage:
Monday, week one. Nandini handed Farida a client report to tidy. Farida said "Sure, ma'am" to every instruction, though she was unsure what the client wanted, and stayed quiet.

Friday, week two. The report came back with red marks. Farida walked to Nandini's desk. "Ma'am, I should have asked earlier. What could I do better next time?" Nandini pulled up a chair and went through it line by line.

Tuesday, week three. Farida brought a new draft with two layouts and a note: "I recommend the second, because the client asked for shorter summaries." Nandini read it and said, "This one is yours." Farida smiled, tired and pleased. 🙂

qa.q: What did Farida say to every instruction on the first Monday?
qa.a: She said "Sure, ma'am" to every instruction.

qa.q: Why did Farida stay quiet in the first week even though she was unsure?
qa.a: She seems to respect Nandini and want to please her, and she was not yet comfortable saying that she did not know what the client wanted.

qa.q: What changed in how Farida brought her work by week three?
qa.a: She brought two layouts with a reasoned recommendation, so she owned the work and offered a solution instead of only waiting for instructions.

qa.q: How might Nandini see the change from week one to week three?
qa.a: Nandini probably sees a junior who now asks, thinks and decides; her words "This one is yours" hint at approval.

grounding: A junior who respects her first manager moves from pleasing silently to asking for feedback, owning her work and proposing solutions.

passage:
"You're pacing. Is it the Monday meeting?" Ganga asked from the sofa.
"The boss walks in with that face and I forget every word. Last week I said nothing about the delayed vendor file."
"Did it get sorted?"
"No. It's still stuck. If I say so, the boss will snap."
"Maybe the face has nothing to do with you. Write it down. Two lines: what is stuck and what you need."
"In an email? Before the meeting?"
"Then it's on record, and you don't have to fight the mood in the room."
Tushar stopped pacing. "Okay. I'll send it tonight. And I'll stop guessing what the face means."
"Good. Now sit. Your tea has gone cold."

qa.q: What was stuck at Tushar's office?
qa.a: The vendor file was delayed and still stuck.

qa.q: Why does Tushar stay silent about the vendor file?
qa.a: Tushar fears the boss will snap, and the boss's face makes every word vanish from Tushar's mind.

qa.q: What could Tushar try so the problem does not blow up later?
qa.a: Send a short email with what is stuck and what is needed before the meeting, so the issue is on record without facing the mood.

qa.q: How might the boss see receiving that email?
qa.a: The boss would likely see a clear, early warning they can act on, rather than a surprise later.

grounding: A junior dreads a moody boss and learns to prepare, write it down and not take moods personally.

passage: I am Naveen, and in my first job at a small print shop I started staying until nine "just this week." Suraj, the owner, said it would count toward my confirmation and that he would sort out overtime pay once the season ended. Three months later it was the same, and nothing was written down. I was tired all the time, but I said nothing because I did not want to seem ungrateful. One evening I described it to an older colleague, Meena. She said, "Ask for it in writing. And find out what the rules say for people in your job, or talk to someone who knows them." I emailed Suraj politely, asking about my hours and pay, and told him I would leave at six from Monday. It was uncomfortable, but for the first time I did not feel alone in it.

qa.q: Until what time did Naveen start staying at the print shop?
qa.a: He started staying until nine.

qa.q: Why did Naveen say nothing for three months?
qa.a: He did not want to seem ungrateful to Suraj, even though he was tired all the time.

qa.q: What steps did Naveen take after talking to Meena?
qa.a: He emailed Suraj politely about his hours and pay, told him he would leave at six from Monday, and had already been told to ask for it in writing and check the rules.

qa.q: How might Suraj see Naveen's email?
qa.a: Suraj may be surprised, since he had promised overtime pay later, and now has to answer in writing instead of with vague promises.

grounding: A young worker made to work late unpaid with vague promises recognises the pattern, sets boundaries and seeks a senior's advice.

passage: Friday evening, the accounts office was half empty when Tanvir stopped at Sudha's desk. "You're my best analyst. Nobody else can fix this month-end file. The whole team will suffer if you're not in tomorrow." Sudha's stomach dropped. Tomorrow was her cousin's engagement lunch. She felt guilty already, and a little flattered too. She had heard the same praise three weekends in a row, and her review still said nothing about extra work. "Sir, will this be counted in my review? And can I take Monday morning off?" Tanvir waved his hand. "We'll see, we'll see." Sudha picked up her bag. "I can do two hours tomorrow morning, not the whole day. After that I have a family event." He frowned, but nodded. 😔

qa.q: Whose engagement lunch was tomorrow?
qa.a: It was Sudha's cousin's engagement lunch.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Sudha have when Tanvir praised her?
qa.a: She felt guilty and a little flattered at the same time, and her stomach dropped.

qa.q: What did Sudha do to test whether the praise was real?
qa.a: She asked whether the extra work would count in her review and whether she could take Monday morning off, then offered a clear limit of two hours.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Sudha's answer?
qa.a: He may feel annoyed, since he frowned, but he still agreed, which suggests her limit was clear enough to accept.

grounding: A boss uses praise and guilt to get extra work; the worker checks the reward and negotiates a clear limit.

passage: Akash sat outside Jahnavi's cabin in the Chennai warehouse office, turning the words over. She had hired him at nineteen with only a diploma, when bigger firms wouldn't call back. He had never forgotten it. But fourteen months had passed, his title still said trainee, and he now handled all the vendor calls. He stood up and knocked. "Ma'am, I'm grateful you gave me this chance, and I'd like to grow here. Can we talk about what it takes to move up from trainee?" Jahnavi raised an eyebrow, then laughed. "I was waiting for you to ask. Let's write a plan." Akash breathed out, noticing that his hands had been clenched the whole time.

qa.q: How long had Akash been a trainee?
qa.a: He had been a trainee for fourteen months.

qa.q: What was Akash worried about before he knocked?
qa.a: He probably feared that asking about his title would seem ungrateful, since he had never forgotten that she gave him the chance.

qa.q: How did Akash combine thanks with a fair question?
qa.a: He first thanked Jahnavi for the chance, then asked plainly what it takes to move up from trainee. 🙂

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see the question?
qa.a: She laughs and says she was waiting for him to ask, so she sees it as normal ambition, not ingratitude.

grounding: A boss gave a young man a chance without a big degree; he is thankful yet asks a fair question about growth.

passage:
Subject: Feedback on my last three tasks

Hi Yusuf,

I have felt that my recent work has not landed well with you, and I would rather ask than guess. Honestly, the short replies in meetings have left me anxious, though I know it may have nothing to do with me. Could we take fifteen minutes this week so you can tell me specifically what needs to change?

For reference, here is what I delivered: the March invoice checks (submitted on the 4th), the vendor sheet (the 11th) and the client call notes (the 18th). I have also asked Deepa in accounts to look at my process, because I would like a second view. If writing is easier, a reply by email works for me.

Thanks for your time.
Reena

qa.q: Which task did Reena submit on the 11th?
qa.a: Reena submitted the vendor sheet on the 11th.

qa.q: What is Reena feeling about the manager's short replies, and how sure is Reena of the cause?
qa.a: Reena feels anxious, yet the email admits the cause may have nothing to do with Reena, so nothing is certain.

qa.q: Why did Reena list the deliveries and ask Deepa to look at the process?
qa.a: The list documents the work with dates, and Deepa gives Reena a second view and another mentor beyond Yusuf. 🙂

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel on reading this email?
qa.a: Yusuf may be surprised or a little uncomfortable, but the polite, specific request makes it easier to give concrete feedback than to stay vague.

grounding: An employee who feels a manager dislikes them asks for concrete feedback, documents the work and seeks another mentor.

passage: At the quarterly all-hands, the manager announced that Naveen had won the recognition award for his client dashboard. People clapped. Suraj clapped too, but something tight sat in his chest. He had built a similar tool two months earlier and nobody had mentioned it. In the pantry afterwards, Kiran muttered, "He just got lucky with the client." Suraj felt the pull of joining in, and let it pass. "Actually, I saw his demo," he said. "The way he showed only three numbers was clever." Back at his desk, he opened Naveen's dashboard and studied the layout. Then he wrote himself a note: finish my own version, and present it at the next review, at my own pace.

qa.q: What did Naveen win the recognition award for?
qa.a: He won it for his client dashboard.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he clapped, and what evidence is there?
qa.a: He felt envy and hurt: something tight sat in his chest because he had built a similar tool that nobody mentioned.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that was better than joining the gossip?
qa.a: He studied Naveen's dashboard and planned to finish and present his own tool at his own pace. 🙂

qa.q: How might Naveen feel if he heard Kiran's remark about luck?
qa.a: He might feel hurt or unfairly dismissed, since his clever three-number demo took real work.

grounding: A colleague gets recognition the protagonist wanted; he studies what the colleague did, keeps his own pace and avoids gossip.

passage:
"Pani puri after work? My treat," Maria said, leaning on Dilnaz's cubicle. "Yes! 😊 Give me ten minutes."
"Okay, also, did you hear who is being moved to the Delhi team?"
"I did, but Kavita told me in confidence, so I'm not repeating it. Even to you."
Maria laughed, a little embarrassed. "Fair. I'd want you to do the same with mine."
"Exactly. And hey, Farhan is new and sits alone at lunch. Should we ask him along on Friday?"
"Just the two of us has been so nice, though."
"It still will be. We can do both." Dilnaz grinned and saved her file.
"Fine, fine. Ten minutes. Bring your umbrella, it looks like rain."

qa.q: What did Maria offer to buy after work?
qa.a: She offered pani puri, her treat.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz refuse to say who was moving to the Delhi team?
qa.a: Kavita told her in confidence, so she wants to keep that trust even with a friend.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz keep the friendship from becoming a clique?
qa.a: She suggests inviting Farhan, who is new and sits alone at lunch, while still keeping time for the two of them.

qa.q: How might Maria feel about being told no on the secret?
qa.a: She is a little embarrassed, but her reply that she would want the same shows she understands and may trust Dilnaz more.

grounding: A colleague becomes a close friend while keeping confidences and avoiding a clique.
